look for discrete, dense white spots that stand out against the softer gray of the lung parenchyma.", "Classify the finding as consistent with healed varicella zoster virus pneumonia if the pattern shows diffuse, random distribution of calcified micronodules, distinguishing it from tuberculosis or histoplasmosis which typically present with upper-lobe predominance or lymphatic distribution."]}, {"category": "diagnosis", "trigger": "When evaluating a chest X-ray with bilateral pulmonary opacities to distinguish Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia from other interstitial or granulomatous lung diseases.", "steps": ["Inspect the distribution of opacities on the PA view, specifically looking for dense consolidations restricted to the peripheral and upper/mid lung zones.", "Verify that the central/perihilar regions and costophrenic angles are relatively spared, creating a 'photographic negative of pulmonary edema' appearance.", "Distinguish from EGPA/Wegener's by noting the absence of cavitation, nodules, or pleural effusions, and from Sarcoidosis by the lack of prominent bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy."]}]

A 31-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious following a car accident. The chest X-ray (Figure 1) showed a large focal density at the left upper lung zone and blunting of the left costophrenic angle. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis based solely on the chest X-ray findings?
A) Left upper lobe pneumonia with pleural effusion
B) Atelectasis of the left upper lobe with pleural effusion
C) Penetrating lung injury from a wooden foreign object
D) Left-sided pneumothorax with pleural effusion
E) Pulmonary contusion with associated pleural effusion
F) Left upper lobe mass with pleural effusion
